newsitem.title: BULGARIA: DELAYED IMF FUNDING WORSENS BULGARIAN OUTLOOK.
newsitem.headline: DELAYED IMF FUNDING WORSENS BULGARIAN OUTLOOK.

text.p: Delay to fulfill structural reform targets agreed with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank postponed desperately needed funding aggravating its economic outlook, officals said on Tuesday.
"It is unlikely that the first programme review will be concluded in September as originaly hoped," IMF Sofia representative Franek Rozwadowski told Reuters.

"There has been a considerable progress in implementing structral reforms but some delays have been experienced particularly in the area of liquidation or rapid privatisation of state owned enterprises," he added.

Bulgaria received the first $115 million tranche in July after sealing a tough reform programme which includes closing scores of loss-making state firms and several insolvent banks, maintaining a tight monetary policy and curbing inflation.
The second $115 million tranche which was due to be disbursed in September will be postponed until the government closes down all loss-makers.

The socialist government, in power since January 1995, pledged to close 68 lossmaking state firms and isolate from credits a further 70 problem enterprises like huge metalworks, mines, the National Electricity Company and the State Railways.
However lack of experience in bankruptcy procedures among local authorities and courts accounted for most of the delays.

"Bankrupting state firms is a completely new experience in this country. Enterprise managers, the courts and even local government oficials were caught unprepared," Industry Minister Lyubomir Dachev told Reuters.
The Industry Ministry is in charge of 38 state firms of the 64 firms earmarked for closure. However only 14 of the loss-makers have been closed so far, said Dachev.
For another nine lossmakers, the regional courts, conceding to pressure from the firms' management or local authorities, have ruled to postpone the closures.
"The courts are exceeding their powers. How can one expect a company which has made losses for years to repay all of its debts in six months," said Dachev.

Industrial firms' losses have been reduced to 2.2 billion in the second half of this year from 7.6 billion levs in 1995 and debts have been cut to 13 billion levs from 18.9 billion levs last year, said Dachev.

Under a financial stabilisation law passed by parliament last month, the 70 problem state companies are expected to present stabilisation programmes to the finance ministry and after their approval reschedule and settle their debts with creidtors by year-end.
Bulgaria's industry is in a vicious circle, said Dachev.

Most of the remaining 1,300 enterprises need short-term lending to fulfill already existing contracts for their products, but most of the country's cash-strapped banks are reluctant to extend credits with the exception of few state-owned banks, he said.
Four months ago the central bank sought to have five major banks declared bankrupt in a bid to offset a grave bank crisis, though the courts will not rule on this unitil mid-September.

"It is time for the ruling socialists to understand that by delaying closures loss-makers they can buy only a short-term political support from a shrinking circle of supporters," said independent think-tank director Krassen Stanchev in a recen interview.
In a bid to raise cash the government accelerated privatisation, which in the past five years was somnolent.
A dozen of the enterprises slated for closure or isolation were sold to local or foreign investors. One of these is the debt-ridden Plama refinery due to be sold to local oil trader Euroenergy.
Sections of Microelectronica electronics plant, another firm marked for shut-down is expected to be sold to four investors, said Dachev, declining to elaborate.
"We will stand ready to move ahead rapidly with the review as soon as these structural measures are implemented providing that a sound macroeconomic framework is in place," said Rozwadowski.
Overshooting of already revised macro-economic targets, which international economists saw as rather optimistic, is inevitable.

A record high key central interest rate of 108 percent, which the central bank has so far refrained from cutting, would entail higher interest payments on domestic debt, which already stands at 150 percent of gross domestic product.
Under a budget revision passed two months ago, the average annual central interest rate is assumed at 67 percent and annual inflation at 104 percent.
Local economists saw annual inflation at around 150 percent as cumulative inflation for the first eight months was 82 percent.
Under the IMF agreement which unblocked crucial funding support to help Bulgaria meet its big foreign debt commitments Bulgaria stands to gain some $580 million over the next 18 months.
However if the reform delays continue default on foreign debt payments was still a real risk next year said international market sources.
-- Sofia Newsroom, 359-2-84561
